vsm2.12:1.1:
It was said above with reference to the mundane kinds of direct-knowledge that this development of concentration
“provides … the benefit of the kinds of direct-knowledge” (XI.122).
vsm2.12:1.2:
Now, in order to perfect those kinds of direct-knowledge the task must be undertaken by a meditator
who has reached the fourth jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, and so on.
vsm2.12:1.3:
And in doing this, not only will this development of concentration have provided
benefits in this way, it will also have become more advanced;
vsm2.12:1.4:
and when he thus possesses concentration so developed as to have both provided benefits and become
more advanced, he will then more easily perfect the development of understanding.
vsm2.12:1.5: So meanwhile we shall deal with the explanation of the kinds of direct-knowledge now.
vsm2.12:2.1:
In order to show the benefits of developing concentration to clansmen whose concentration has reached the fourth
jhāna, and in order to teach progressively refined Dhamma, five kinds of mundane direct-knowledge have been described by the Blessed
One. They are: (1) the kinds of supernormal power, described in the way beginning, “When his concentrated mind is thus purified,
bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, and has become malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability,
he directs, he inclines, his mind to the kinds of supernormal power. He wields the various kinds of supernormal power. Having
been one, he becomes many …” (D I 77); (2) the knowledge of the divine ear element; (3) the knowledge of penetration of minds;
(4) the knowledge of recollection of past lives; and (5) the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.
vsm2.12:3.1:
If a meditator wants to begin performing the transformation by supernormal power described as, “Having been one, he becomes many,”
etc., he must achieve the eight attainments in each of the eight kasiṇas ending with the white kasiṇa.
vsm2.12:3.2:
He must also have complete control of his mind in the following fourteen ways: (i) in the order of the kasiṇa,
(ii) in the reverse order of the kasiṇa, (iii) in the order and reverse order of the kasiṇa, (iv) in the order of the jhāna,
(v) in the reverse order of the jhāna (vi) in the order and reverse order of the jhāna, (vii) skipping jhāna,
(viii) skipping kasiṇa, (ix) skipping jhāna and kasiṇa, (x) transposition of factors, (xi) transposition of object,
(xii) transposition of factors and object, (xiii) definition of factors, and (xiv) definition of object.
vsm2.12:3.3: But what is “in the order of the kasiṇa” here? What is “definition of object”?
vsm2.12:3.4:
(i) Here a bhikkhu attains jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, after that in the water kasiṇa, and so progressing
through the eight kasiṇas, doing so even a hundred times, even a thousand times, in each one.
vsm2.12:3.5: This is called in the order of the kasiṇas.
vsm2.12:3.6: (ii) Attaining them in like manner in reverse order, starting with the white kasiṇa, is called in the reverse order of the kasiṇas.
vsm2.12:3.7:
(iii) Attaining them again and again in forward and reverse order, from the earth kasiṇa
up to the white kasiṇa and from the white kasiṇa back to the earth kasiṇa,
vsm2.12:3.8: is called in the order and reverse order of the kasiṇas.
vsm2.12:4.1:
(iv) Attaining again and again from the first jhāna up to the base consisting of neither
perception nor non-perception is called in the order of the jhānas.
vsm2.12:4.2:
(v) Attaining again and again from the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception
back to the first jhāna is called in the reverse order of the jhānas.
vsm2.12:4.3:
(vi) Attaining in forward and reverse order, from the first jhāna up to the base consisting of neither perception nor
non-perception and from the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception back to the first jhāna,
vsm2.12:4.4: is called in the order and reverse order of the jhānas.
vsm2.12:5.1:
(vii) He skips alternate jhānas without skipping the kasiṇas in the following way: having first attained the first
jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, he attains the third jhāna in that same kasiṇa, and after that, having removed the kasiṇa (X.6),
he attains the base consisting of boundless space, after that the base consisting of nothingness.
vsm2.12:5.3: And that based on the water kasiṇa, etc., should be construed similarly.
vsm2.12:5.4:
(viii) When he skips alternate kasiṇas without skipping jhānas in the following way: having attained the first jhāna in the earth
kasiṇa, he again attains that same jhāna in the fire kasiṇa and then in the blue kasiṇa and then in the red kasiṇa,
vsm2.12:5.6:
(ix) When he skips both jhānas and kasiṇas in the following way: having attained the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa,
he next attains the third in the fire kasiṇa, next the base consisting of boundless space after removing
the blue kasiṇa, next the base consisting of nothingness arrived at from the red kasiṇa,
vsm2.12:5.7: this is called skipping jhānas and kasiṇas.
vsm2.12:6.1:
(x) Attaining the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa and then attaining the others in that same
kasiṇa is called transposition of factors.
vsm2.12:6.2: (xi) Attaining the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa and then that same jhāna in the water kasiṇa … in the white kasiṇa
vsm2.12:6.4:
(xii) Transposition of object and factors together takes place in the following way:
he attains the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, the second jhāna in the water kasiṇa,
vsm2.12:6.5: the third in the fire kasiṇa,
vsm2.12:6.6: the fourth in the air kasiṇa,
vsm2.12:6.7: the base consisting of boundless space by removing the blue kasiṇa,
vsm2.12:6.8: the base consisting of boundless consciousness arrived at from the yellow kasiṇa,
vsm2.12:6.9: the base consisting of nothingness from the red kasiṇa,
vsm2.12:6.10: and the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception from the white kasiṇa.
vsm2.12:6.11: This is called transposition of factors and object.
vsm2.12:7.1:
(xiii) The defining of only the jhāna factors by defining the first jhāna as five-factored, the second
as three-factored, the third as two-factored, and likewise the fourth, the base consisting of boundless
space, … and the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception,
vsm2.12:7.3:
(xiv) Likewise, the defining of only the object as “This is the earth kasiṇa,” “This is the water
kasiṇa” … “This is the white kasiṇa,” is called definition of object.
vsm2.12:7.4: Some would also have “defining of factors and object”;
vsm2.12:7.5: but since that is not given in the commentaries it is certainly not a heading in the development.
vsm2.12:8.1:
It is not possible for a meditator to begin to accomplish transformation by supernormal powers unless he
has previously completed his development by controlling his mind in these fourteen ways.
vsm2.12:8.2: Now, the kasiṇa preliminary work is difficult for a beginner and only one in a hundred or a thousand can do it.
vsm2.12:8.3: The arousing of the sign is difficult for one who has done the preliminary work and only one in a hundred or a thousand can do it.
vsm2.12:8.4: To extend the sign when it has arisen and to reach absorption is difficult and only one in a hundred or a thousand can do it.
vsm2.12:8.5: To tame one’s mind in the fourteen ways after reaching absorption is difficult and only one in a hundred or a thousand can do it.
vsm2.12:8.6:
The transformation by supernormal power after training one’s mind in the fourteen ways
is difficult and only one in a hundred or a thousand can do it.
vsm2.12:8.7: Rapid response after attaining transformation is difficult and only one in a hundred or a thousand can do it.
vsm2.12:9.1:
Like the Elder Rakkhita who, eight years after his full admission to the Order, was in the midst of thirty thousand bhikkhus
possessing supernormal powers who had come to attend upon the sickness of the Elder Mahā-Rohaṇa-Gutta at Therambatthala.
vsm2.12:9.2: His feat is mentioned under the earth kasiṇa (IV.135).
vsm2.12:9.3:
Seeing his feat, an elder said, “Friends, if Rakkhita had not been there, we should have been put to shame.
It could have been said, ‘They were unable to protect the royal nāga.’
vsm2.12:9.4:
So we ourselves ought to go about with our abilities perfected, just as it
is proper (for soldiers) to go about with weapons cleaned of stains.”
vsm2.12:9.5: The thirty thousand bhikkhus heeded the elder’s advice and achieved rapid response.
vsm2.12:10.1: And helping another after acquiring rapidity in responding is difficult and only one in a hundred or a thousand can do it.
vsm2.12:10.2:
Like the elder who gave protection against the rain of embers by creating earth in the sky,
when the rain of embers was produced by Māra at the Giribhaṇḍavahana offering.
vsm2.12:11.1:
It is only in Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, chief disciples, etc., who have vast previous endeavour behind them,
that this transformation by supernormal power and other such special qualities as the discriminations are brought to success
simply with the attainment of Arahantship and without the progressive course of development of the kind just described.
vsm2.12:12.1:
So just as when a goldsmith wants to make some kind of ornament, he does so only after
making the gold malleable and wieldy by smelting it, etc.,
vsm2.12:12.2: and just as when a potter wants to make some kind of vessel, he does so only after making the clay well kneaded and malleable,
vsm2.12:12.3: a beginner too must likewise prepare for the kinds of supernormal powers by controlling his mind in these fourteen ways;
vsm2.12:12.4:
and he must do so also by making his mind malleable and wieldy both by attaining under the headings of zeal,
consciousness, energy, and inquiry, and by mastery in adverting, and so on.
vsm2.12:12.5:
But one who already has the required condition for it owing to practice in previous lives needs
only prepare himself by acquiring mastery in the fourth jhāna in the kasiṇas.
vsm2.12:13.1: Now, the Blessed One showed how the preparation should be done in saying, “When his concentrated mind,” and so on.
vsm2.12:13.2: Here is the explanation, which follows the text (see §2).
vsm2.12:13.3: Herein, he is a meditator who has attained the fourth jhāna.
vsm2.12:13.4: Thus signifies the order in which the fourth jhāna comes;
vsm2.12:13.5: having obtained the fourth jhāna in this order beginning with attaining the first jhāna, is what is meant.
vsm2.12:13.6: Concentrated: concentrated by means of the fourth jhāna.
vsm2.12:14.1: But as to the words “purified,” etc., it is purified by means of the state of mindfulness purified by equanimity.
vsm2.12:14.2: It is bright precisely because it is purified; it is limpid (see A I 10), is what is meant.
vsm2.12:14.3:
It is unblemished since the blemishes consisting of greed, etc.,
are eliminated by the removal of their conditions consisting of bliss, and the rest.
vsm2.12:14.4: It is rid of defilement precisely because it is unblemished; for it is by the blemish that the consciousness becomes defiled.
vsm2.12:14.5: It has become malleable because it is well developed; it suffers mastery, is what is meant,
vsm2.12:14.6: for consciousness that suffers mastery is called “malleable.”
vsm2.12:14.7: It is wieldy (kammanīya) precisely because it is malleable;
vsm2.12:14.8: it suffers being worked (kammakkhama), is fit to be worked (kammayogga), is what is meant.
vsm2.12:15.1: For a malleable consciousness is wieldy, like well-smelted gold;
vsm2.12:15.2: and it is both of these because it is well developed, according as it is said:
vsm2.12:15.3: “Bhikkhus, I do not see anyone thing that, when developed and cultivated, becomes so malleable and wieldy as does the mind” (A I 9).
vsm2.12:16.1: It is steady because it is steadied in this purifiedness, and the rest.
vsm2.12:16.2: It is attained to imperturbability (āneñjappatta) precisely because it is steady;
vsm2.12:16.3: it is motionless, without perturbation (niriñjana), is what is meant.
vsm2.12:16.4: Or alternatively, it is steady because steady in its own masterability through malleability and wieldiness,
vsm2.12:16.5: and it is attained to imperturbability because it is reinforced by faith, and so on.
vsm2.12:17.1: For consciousness reinforced by faith is not perturbed by faithlessness;
vsm2.12:17.2: when reinforced by energy, it is not perturbed by idleness;
vsm2.12:17.3: when reinforced by mindfulness, it is not perturbed by negligence;
vsm2.12:17.4: when reinforced by concentration, it is not perturbed by agitation;
vsm2.12:17.5: when reinforced by understanding, it is not perturbed by ignorance;
vsm2.12:17.6: and when illuminated, it is not perturbed by the darkness of defilement.
vsm2.12:17.7: So when it is reinforced by these six states, it is attained to imperturbability.
vsm2.12:18.1:
Consciousness possessing these eight factors in this way is susceptible of being directed
to the realization by direct-knowledge of states realizable by direct-knowledge.
vsm2.12:19.1: Another method: It is concentrated by means of fourth-jhāna concentration.
vsm2.12:19.2: It is purified by separation from the hindrances.
vsm2.12:19.3: It is bright owing to the surmounting of applied thought and the rest.
vsm2.12:19.4: It is unblemished owing to absence of evil wishes based on the obtainment of jhāna.
vsm2.12:19.5: It is rid of defilement owing to the disappearance of the defilements of the mind consisting in covetousness, etc.;
vsm2.12:19.6: and both of these should be understood according to the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta (MN 5) and the Vattha Sutta (MN 7).
vsm2.12:19.7: It is become malleable by masterability.
vsm2.12:19.8: It is wieldy by reaching the state of a road to power (§50).
vsm2.12:19.9: It is steady and attained to imperturbability by reaching the refinement of completed development;
vsm2.12:19.10: the meaning is that according as it has attained imperturbability so it is steady.
vsm2.12:19.11:
And the consciousness possessing these eight factors in this way is susceptible of being directed to the realization
by direct-knowledge of states realizable by direct-knowledge, since it is the basis, the proximate cause, for them.
vsm2.12:20.1:
He directs, he inclines, his mind to the kinds of supernormal powers (iddhi-vidha—lit. “kinds of success”): here “success”
(iddhi) is the success of succeeding (ijjhana); in the sense of production, in the sense of obtainment, is what is meant.
vsm2.12:20.2: For what is produced and obtained is called “successful,”
vsm2.12:20.3: according as it is said, “When a mortal desires, if his desire is fulfilled” (samijjhati) (Sn 766),
vsm2.12:20.4:
and likewise: “Renunciation succeeds (ijjhati), thus it is a success (iddhi) … It metamorphoses (paṭiharati) lust,
thus it is a metamorphosis (pāṭihāriya) … The Arahant path succeeds, thus it is a success … It
metamorphoses all defilements, thus it is a metamorphosis” (Paṭis II 229).
vsm2.12:21.1: Another method: success is in the sense of succeeding.
vsm2.12:21.2:
That is a term for the effectiveness of the means; for effectiveness of the means
succeeds with the production of the result intended,
vsm2.12:21.3:
according as it is said: “This householder Citta is virtuous and magnanimous. If he should aspire, ‘Let me in the future
become a Wheel-turning Monarch,’ being virtuous, he will succeed in his aspiration, because it is purified” (S IV 303).
vsm2.12:22.1: Another method: beings succeed by its means, thus it is success.
vsm2.12:22.2: They succeed, thus they are successful; they are enriched, promoted, is what is meant.
vsm2.12:22.3: That success (power) is of ten kinds, according as it is said, “Kinds of success: ten kinds of success,”
vsm2.12:22.4:
after which it is said further, “What ten kinds of success? Success by resolve, success as transformation,
success as the mind-made body, success by intervention of knowledge, success by intervention of concentration,
Noble Ones’ success, success born of kamma result, success of the meritorious, success through the sciences,
success in the sense of succeeding due to right exertion applied here or there” (Paṭis II 205).
vsm2.12:23.1:
(i) Herein, the success shown in the exposition of the above summary thus, “Normally one, he adverts to himself as many
or a hundred or a thousand or a hundred thousand; having adverted, he resolves with knowledge, “Let me be many” (Paṭis II 207),
vsm2.12:23.2: is called success by resolve because it is produced by resolving.
vsm2.12:24.1:
(ii) That given as follows, “Having abandoned his normal form, he shows himself in the form of a boy
or the form of a serpent … or he shows a manifold military array” (Paṭis II 210),
vsm2.12:24.2: is called success as transformation because of the abandoning and alteration of the normal form.
vsm2.12:25.1:
(iii) That given in this way, “Here a bhikkhu creates out of this body another body
possessing visible form, mind-made” (Paṭis II 210),
vsm2.12:25.2: is called success as the mind-made (body) because it occurs as the production of another, mind-made, body inside the body.
